claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) is an important noradrenergic nucleus that has recently attracted attention because of its emerging role in cognitive and psychiatric disorders.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) is an important noradrenergic nucleus that has recently attracted a lot of attention because of its emerging role in cognitive and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement about the LC's importance and recent research focus, supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Previous histological studies have shown that the LC has heterogeneous connections and cellular features.
source: Although previous histological studies have shown that the LC has heterogeneous connections and cellular features, no studies have yet assessed its functional topography in vivo, how this heterogeneity changes over aging, and whether it is associated with cognition and mood.
evidence: This claim references previous histological studies, indicating it is supported by prior research cited in the literature.

claim: No studies have yet assessed the LC's functional topography in vivo, how this heterogeneity changes over aging, and whether it is associated with cognition and mood.
source: Although previous histological studies have shown that the LC has heterogeneous connections and cellular features, no studies have yet assessed its functional topography in vivo, how this heterogeneity changes over aging, and whether it is associated with cognition and mood.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The study employed a gradient-based approach to characterize the functional heterogeneity in the organization of the LC over aging using 3T resting-state fMRI in the CamCAN cohort (n=618, aged 18-88 years).
source: Here, we employ a gradient-based approach to characterize the functional heterogeneity in the organization of the LC over aging using 3T resting-state fMRI in a population-based cohort aged from 18 to 88 years of age (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience cohort, n=618).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The LC exhibits a rostro-caudal functional gradient along its longitudinal axis.
source: We show that the LC exhibits a rostro-caudal functional gradient along its longitudinal axis, which was replicated in an independent dataset (Human Connectome Project [HCP] 7T dataset, n=184).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data from the CamCAN cohort and replicated in the HCP dataset.

claim: The rostro-caudal functional gradient of the LC was replicated in an independent dataset (HCP 7T dataset, n=184).
source: We show that the LC exhibits a rostro-caudal functional gradient along its longitudinal axis, which was replicated in an independent dataset (Human Connectome Project [HCP] 7T dataset, n=184).
evidence: This claim is supported by replication of findings in a second independent dataset.

claim: The main rostro-caudal direction of the LC gradient was consistent across age groups.
source: Although the main rostro-caudal direction of this gradient was consistent across age groups, its spatial features varied with increasing age, emotional memory, and emotion regulation.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the CamCAN cohort across different age groups.

claim: The spatial features of the LC gradient varied with increasing age, emotional memory, and emotion regulation.
source: Although the main rostro-caudal direction of this gradient was consistent across age groups, its spatial features varied with increasing age, emotional memory, and emotion regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analyses of the relationship between gradient features and behavioral measures.

claim: A loss of rostral-like connectivity, more clustered functional topography, and greater asymmetry between right and left LC gradients was associated with higher age.
source: More specifically, a loss of rostral-like connectivity, more clustered functional topography, and greater asymmetry between right and left LC gradients was associated with higher age and worse behavioral performance.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analyses showing correlations between gradient parameters and age.

claim: A loss of rostral-like connectivity, more clustered functional topography, and greater asymmetry between right and left LC gradients was associated with worse behavioral performance.
source: More specifically, a loss of rostral-like connectivity, more clustered functional topography, and greater asymmetry between right and left LC gradients was associated with higher age and worse behavioral performance.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analyses showing correlations between gradient parameters and behavioral measures.

claim: Participants with higher-than-normal Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) ratings exhibited alterations in the LC gradient that manifested in greater asymmetry.
source: Furthermore, participants with higher-than-normal Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) ratings exhibited alterations in the gradient as well, which manifested in greater asymmetry.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical comparison of gradient features between groups with normal and elevated HADS scores.

claim: Most of the noradrenergic transmission in the brain originates from the locus coeruleus (LC).
source: Most of the noradrenergic transmission in the brain originates from the locus coeruleus (LC), a bilateral nucleus in the dorsolateral pons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the LC's role in the brain.

claim: The LC is a bilateral nucleus in the dorsolateral pons.
source: Most of the noradrenergic transmission in the brain originates from the locus coeruleus (LC), a bilateral nucleus in the dorsolateral pons.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact about the LC's location.

claim: The LC has been implicated in aging-related cognitive changes and neurodegenerative conditions, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) or Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: The LC has been implicated in aging-related cognitive changes and neurodegenerative conditions, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) or Parkinson's disease (PD) (Betts et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Different conditions seem to affect different parts of the LC.
source: Interestingly, different conditions seem to affect different parts of the LC (Madelung et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2022), and several studies show that subregions of the LC might be involved in different cognitive functions and psychiatric symptoms (Hämmerer et al., 2018; Ciampa et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Subregions of the LC might be involved in different cognitive functions and psychiatric symptoms.
source: Interestingly, different conditions seem to affect different parts of the LC (Madelung et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2022), and several studies show that subregions of the LC might be involved in different cognitive functions and psychiatric symptoms (Hämmerer et al., 2018; Ciampa et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The rostral part of the LC is associated with memory and emotion regulation.
source: Specifically, the rostral part is associated with memory and emotion regulation, being often affected in AD (Hämmerer et al., 2018; Ciampa et al., 2022; Betts et al., 2019a; Theofilas et al., 2017), whereas the integrity of the caudal part has been linked to more general cognitive processes in PD (Ye et al., 2022; Doppler et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The rostral part of the LC is often affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Specifically, the rostral part is associated with memory and emotion regulation, being often affected in AD (Hämmerer et al., 2018; Ciampa et al., 2022; Betts et al., 2019a; Theofilas et al., 2017), whereas the integrity of the caudal part has been linked to more general cognitive processes in PD (Ye et al., 2022; Doppler et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The integrity of the caudal part of the LC has been linked to more general cognitive processes in Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Specifically, the rostral part is associated with memory and emotion regulation, being often affected in AD (Hämmerer et al., 2018; Ciampa et al., 2022; Betts et al., 2019a; Theofilas et al., 2017), whereas the integrity of the caudal part has been linked to more general cognitive processes in PD (Ye et al., 2022; Doppler et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A dichotomous functional division model of the LC might be oversimplistic.
source: However, a dichotomous functional division model of the LC might be oversimplistic, and technical difficulties concerning imaging of the LC (such as low spatial resolution of functional imaging techniques, inconvenient anatomical location, or noise from adjacent cerebrospinal fluid spaces; Engels-Domínguez et al., 2023) could hide a more complex underlying functional organization.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of current models, supported by reasoning about technical challenges.

claim: Technical difficulties concerning imaging of the LC (such as low spatial resolution of functional imaging techniques, inconvenient anatomical location, or noise from adjacent cerebrospinal fluid spaces) could hide a more complex underlying functional organization.
source: However, a dichotomous functional division model of the LC might be oversimplistic, and technical difficulties concerning imaging of the LC (such as low spatial resolution of functional imaging techniques, inconvenient anatomical location, or noise from adjacent cerebrospinal fluid spaces; Engels-Domínguez et al., 2023) could hide a more complex underlying functional organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation discussing technical challenges in LC imaging.

claim: Multiple overlapping axes of functional organization might be present in the LC that can confound current traditional cluster-based models.
source: Additionally, multiple overlapping axes of functional organization might be present that can confound current traditional cluster-based models that seek to divide the LC into subregions (Haak and Beckmann, 2020; Poe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The hippocampus is organized by a gradient of connectivity profiles and microstructural properties along its longitudinal axis.
source: For example, several studies reported that the hippocampus is organized by a gradient of connectivity profiles and microstructural properties along its longitudinal axis (Przeździk et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on hippocampal gradients.

claim: Spatial characteristics of hippocampal gradients explained individual differences in behavior better than a cluster-based model.
source: These spatial characteristics of hippocampal gradients explained individual differences in behavior better than a cluster-based model, and therefore provided a closer approximation to the true organization profile of this region.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited hippocampal gradient studies.

claim: A second axis of connectopic organization was present in the striatum that closely resembled the spatial distribution of dopamine transporters across different medication and symptomatology stages in Parkinson's disease.
source: Oldehinkel et al. found that, apart from the primary functional connectivity gradient, a second axis of connectopic organization was present in the striatum that closely resembled the spatial distribution of dopamine transporters across different medication and symptomatology stages, providing a non-invasive marker for striatal dopamine transporter density in PD (Oldehinkel et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: No studies have investigated the functional gradients of the LC.
source: To our knowledge, so far, no studies have investigated the functional gradients of the LC.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge of existing research.

claim: The LC modulates various behavioral functions and widespread brain regions in a very precise manner.
source: This is important because this region modulates various behavioral functions and widespread brain regions in a very precise manner (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Studies using fMRI to describe connectivity in the LC report heterogeneous results, possibly because the localization methods, the studied populations, and preprocessing pipelines often differ.
source: Furthermore, studies using fMRI to describe connectivity in the LC report heterogeneous results – possibly because the localization methods, the studied populations, and preprocessing pipelines often differ (Liebe et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Liebe et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2016) – and a similarity gradient-based approach might be better suited to characterize its functional organization by mitigating the effect of heterogeneous individual differences in connectivity and imaging acquisition-related noise, since it is less affected by, for example, region of interest (ROI) inaccuracies (Haak et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and includes speculation about the reasons for heterogeneity.

claim: A similarity gradient-based approach might be better suited to characterize the LC's functional organization by mitigating the effect of heterogeneous individual differences in connectivity and imaging acquisition-related noise.
source: Furthermore, studies using fMRI to describe connectivity in the LC report heterogeneous results – possibly because the localization methods, the studied populations, and preprocessing pipelines often differ (Liebe et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Liebe et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2016) – and a similarity gradient-based approach might be better suited to characterize its functional organization by mitigating the effect of heterogeneous individual differences in connectivity and imaging acquisition-related noise, since it is less affected by, for example, region of interest (ROI) inaccuracies (Haak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the advantages of the gradient-based approach, supported by a citation.

claim: The average dominant gradient consistently exhibited a rostro-caudal organization in all age groups in the CamCAN dataset and across all subjects in the HCP 7T dataset.
source: The average dominant gradient consistently exhibited a rostro-caudal organization in all age groups in the CamCAN dataset and across all subjects in the HCP 7T dataset (see Figure 1A; also see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a difference map of gradients from the two datasets).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data from both cohorts and visualized in figures.

claim: Gradients using a larger LC ROI from Tona et al., 2017 retained the rostro-caudal organization.
source: To assess the extent to which the ROI mask influences the rostro-caudal gradient, we repeated the gradient calculation in both datasets using a larger LC ROI from Tona et al., 2017; gradients using this ROI retained the rostro-caudal organization (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a validation finding showing robustness of the gradient to different ROI definitions.

claim: The LC gradient was monotonous, meaning that the stepwise changes in connectivity were consistent along the longitudinal axis of the LC and did not show clear functional area boundaries.
source: The gradient was monotonous, meaning that the stepwise changes in connectivity were consistent along the longitudinal axis of the LC and did not show clear functional area boundaries.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about the nature of the gradient based on data analysis.

claim: When partitioned into rostral and caudal parts, the rostral part of the LC was characterized by connections to the posterior and anterior cingulate cortices and the medial temporal lobe.
source: When partitioned into rostral and caudal parts, the rostral part was characterized by connections to the posterior and anterior cingulate cortices and the medial temporal lobe, whereas the caudal part projected to the parietal and visual cortices.
evidence: This is a finding about connectivity patterns derived from data analysis.

claim: The caudal part of the LC projected to the parietal and visual cortices.
source: When partitioned into rostral and caudal parts, the rostral part was characterized by connections to the posterior and anterior cingulate cortices and the medial temporal lobe, whereas the caudal part projected to the parietal and visual cortices.
evidence: This is a finding about connectivity patterns derived from data analysis.

claim: The rostral LC mainly projected to the hippocampi, amygdalae, and striatum.
source: Regarding subcortical structures, the rostral LC mainly projected to the hippocampi, amygdalae, and striatum, while the caudal part projected to the thalami, occipital, precentral, and postcentral regions (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding about subcortical connectivity patterns derived from data analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: The caudal part of the LC projected to the thalami, occipital, precentral, and postcentral regions.
source: Regarding subcortical structures, the rostral LC mainly projected to the hippocampi, amygdalae, and striatum, while the caudal part projected to the thalami, occipital, precentral, and postcentral regions (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding about subcortical connectivity patterns derived from data analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: The rostral part of the LC was mainly associated with higher order, associative cortical areas and limbic regions.
source: To summarize, the rostral part was mainly associated with higher order, associative cortical areas and limbic regions, while the caudal part was more connected to primary sensorimotor and visual areas.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: The caudal part of the LC was more connected to primary sensorimotor and visual areas.
source: To summarize, the rostral part was mainly associated with higher order, associative cortical areas and limbic regions, while the caudal part was more connected to primary sensorimotor and visual areas.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance in age over and above the effects of sex (F=8.671, adjusted partial R2=0.504, p<0.001).
source: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance in age over and above the effects of sex (F=8.671, adjusted partial R2=0.504, p<0.001; see Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of the relationship between gradient features and age.

claim: Specific parameters of the gradient's spatial model were associated with age in a way that a loss of rostral-like connectivity, more clustered appearance, and increased asymmetry were related with older age.
source: Also, specific parameters of the gradient's spatial model were associated with age in a way that a loss of rostral-like connectivity, more clustered appearance, and increased asymmetry were related with older age (see correlation plots on Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of gradient parameters and age, visualized in figures.

claim: With increasing age, the gradient could be clustered into rostral and caudal regions more effectively (R=0.313, p<0.009).
source: This was further confirmed by the clusterability analysis, which showed that, with increasing age, the gradient could be clustered into rostral and caudal regions more effectively (R=0.313, p<0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from clusterability analysis.

claim: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory recollection scores (F=2.632, adjusted partial R2=0.224, p=0.016).
source: Regarding cognitive variables, the gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory scores – more specifically recollection of stimulus valence (F=2.632, adjusted partial R2=0.224, p=0.016), recognition of previously seen objects associated with emotionally charged stimuli (F=7.992, adjusted partial R2=0.552, p<0.001), priming (F=2.198, adjusted partial R2=0.175, p=0.042), emotional reactivity to negative events (F=4.008, adjusted partial R2=0.365, p<0.001), and reappraisal of emotional valence for negative stimuli (F=2.827, adjusted partial R2=0.259, p=0.012) after false discovery rate (FDR) corrections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of the relationship between gradient features and cognitive measures.

claim: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory recognition scores (F=7.992, adjusted partial R2=0.552, p<0.001).
source: Regarding cognitive variables, the gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory scores – more specifically recollection of stimulus valence (F=2.632, adjusted partial R2=0.224, p=0.016), recognition of previously seen objects associated with emotionally charged stimuli (F=7.992, adjusted partial R2=0.552, p<0.001), priming (F=2.198, adjusted partial R2=0.175, p=0.042), emotional reactivity to negative events (F=4.008, adjusted partial R2=0.365, p<0.001), and reappraisal of emotional valence for negative stimuli (F=2.827, adjusted partial R2=0.259, p=0.012) after false discovery rate (FDR) corrections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of the relationship between gradient features and cognitive measures.

claim: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory priming scores (F=2.198, adjusted partial R2=0.175, p=0.042).
source: Regarding cognitive variables, the gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory scores – more specifically recollection of stimulus valence (F=2.632, adjusted partial R2=0.224, p=0.016), recognition of previously seen objects associated with emotionally charged stimuli (F=7.992, adjusted partial R2=0.552, p<0.001), priming (F=2.198, adjusted partial R2=0.175, p=0.042), emotional reactivity to negative events (F=4.008, adjusted partial R2=0.365, p<0.001), and reappraisal of emotional valence for negative stimuli (F=2.827, adjusted partial R2=0.259, p=0.012) after false discovery rate (FDR) corrections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of the relationship between gradient features and cognitive measures.

claim: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional reactivity to negative events (F=4.008, adjusted partial R2=0.365, p<0.001).
source: Regarding cognitive variables, the gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory scores – more specifically recollection of stimulus valence (F=2.632, adjusted partial R2=0.224, p=0.016), recognition of previously seen objects associated with emotionally charged stimuli (F=7.992, adjusted partial R2=0.552, p<0.001), priming (F=2.198, adjusted partial R2=0.175, p=0.042), emotional reactivity to negative events (F=4.008, adjusted partial R2=0.365, p<0.001), and reappraisal of emotional valence for negative stimuli (F=2.827, adjusted partial R2=0.259, p=0.012) after false discovery rate (FDR) corrections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of the relationship between gradient features and cognitive measures.

claim: The gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in reappraisal of emotional valence for negative stimuli (F=2.827, adjusted partial R2=0.259, p=0.012).
source: Regarding cognitive variables, the gradient explained a significant amount of variance above the effects of age, sex, and education in emotional memory scores – more specifically recollection of stimulus valence (F=2.632, adjusted partial R2=0.224, p=0.016), recognition of previously seen objects associated with emotionally charged stimuli (F=7.992, adjusted partial R2=0.552, p<0.001), priming (F=2.198, adjusted partial R2=0.175, p=0.042), emotional reactivity to negative events (F=4.008, adjusted partial R2=0.365, p<0.001), and reappraisal of emotional valence for negative stimuli (F=2.827, adjusted partial R2=0.259, p=0.012) after false discovery rate (FDR) corrections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of the relationship between gradient features and cognitive measures.

claim: An old-like functional gradient exhibiting a loss of rostral-like connectivity and more clustered functional organization was associated with worse performance in emotional memory and emotion regulation tasks related to negative events.
source: In general, an old-like functional gradient exhibiting a loss of rostral-like connectivity and more clustered functional organization was associated with worse performance in emotional memory and emotion regulation tasks related to negative events.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings relating gradient features to behavioral performance.

claim: Overall spatial features of LC functional gradients did not explain a significant amount of additional variance in executive functions (Hotel-task; F=1.473, adjusted partial R2=0.036, p<0.168).
source: Overall spatial features of LC functional gradients did not explain a significant amount of additional variance in executive functions (Hotel-task; F=1.473, adjusted partial R2=0.036, p<0.168) or sleep quality scores (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index [PSQI]; F=1.124, adjusted partial R2=0.01, p<0.352).
evidence: This is a negative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Overall spatial features of LC functional gradients did not explain a significant amount of additional variance in sleep quality scores (PSQI; F=1.124, adjusted partial R2=0.01, p<0.352).
source: Overall spatial features of LC functional gradients did not explain a significant amount of additional variance in executive functions (Hotel-task; F=1.473, adjusted partial R2=0.036, p<0.168) or sleep quality scores (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index [PSQI]; F=1.124, adjusted partial R2=0.01, p<0.352).
evidence: This is a negative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Participants with higher-than-normal HADS scores exhibited a different gradient compared to participants with normal HADS scores (one-way MANOVA: p<0.001).
source: Participants with higher-than-normal HADS scores exhibited a different gradient compared to participants with normal HADS scores (one-way multivariate analysis of variance [MANOVA]: p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from group comparison analysis.

claim: The gradient in the pathological group (high HADS scores) showed generally less rostral-like connectivity and was more asymmetric.
source: The gradient in the pathological group showed generally less rostral-like connectivity and was more asymmetric (left LC – z: p<0.002, z3: p<0.007; right LC – x: p<0.001, z: p<0.001, x3: p<0.001, z3: p<0.001; see Figure 4), showing a further reduction of left rostral-like connectivity compared to the right one.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison between groups with different HADS scores.

claim: High HADS scores were associated with a further reduction of left rostral-like connectivity compared to the right one.
source: The gradient in the pathological group showed generally less rostral-like connectivity and was more asymmetric (left LC – z: p<0.002, z3: p<0.007; right LC – x: p<0.001, z: p<0.001, x3: p<0.001, z3: p<0.001; see Figure 4), showing a further reduction of left rostral-like connectivity compared to the right one.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison between groups with different HADS scores.

claim: A rostral-caudal division has already been reported in the LC by studies using structural imaging and LC-contrast MRI sequences.
source: A rostral-caudal division has already been reported in the LC by studies using structural imaging and LC-contrast MRI sequences (Dahl et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The rostral-caudal division in the LC seems to be driven by a heterogeneous distribution of cellular, molecular, and connectivity-related characteristics along the LC.
source: This division seems to be driven by a heterogeneous distribution of cellular, molecular, and connectivity-related characteristics along the LC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature and the current findings.

claim: LC-contrast MRI sequences such as magnetization transfer imaging seem to be associated with neuronal integrity in the LC.
source: Specifically, LC-contrast MRI sequences such as magnetization transfer imaging seem to be associated with neuronal integrity in the LC, although the biological sources of this contrast are still not fully understood (Keren et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and includes acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: The biological sources of LC-contrast in magnetization transfer imaging are still not fully understood.
source: Specifically, LC-contrast MRI sequences such as magnetization transfer imaging seem to be associated with neuronal integrity in the LC, although the biological sources of this contrast are still not fully understood (Keren et al., 2015).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in current understanding, supported by a citation.

claim: A post-mortem study showed that noradrenergic neural somas in the LC show a specific distribution characterized by a dense collection of cell bodies in the central LC that disperses in both caudal and rostral directions.
source: A post-mortem study showed that noradrenergic neural somas in the LC show a specific distribution characterized by a dense collection of cell bodies in the central LC that disperses in both caudal and rostral directions, with a lower number of these noradrenergic cells in the caudal part compared to the rostral part (Fernandes et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a post-mortem study.

claim: There is a lower number of noradrenergic cells in the caudal part of the LC compared to the rostral part.
source: A post-mortem study showed that noradrenergic neural somas in the LC show a specific distribution characterized by a dense collection of cell bodies in the central LC that disperses in both caudal and rostral directions, with a lower number of these noradrenergic cells in the caudal part compared to the rostral part (Fernandes et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a post-mortem study.

claim: Using a gradient-based approach applied to functional imaging, the study reproduced the structural rostral-caudal division, revealing for the first time a rostro-caudal functional organization consistent across cohorts with different acquisition parameters.
source: Using a gradient-based approach applied to functional imaging, we reproduced this structural division, revealing for the first time a rostro-caudal functional organization consistent across cohorts with different acquisition parameters.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary contribution, supported by the data presented.

claim: Tracer studies show that the rostral-dorsal part of the LC projects to neocortical regions, the hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, and amygdala.
source: Tracer studies show that the rostral-dorsal part of the LC projects to neocortical regions, the hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, and amygdala, whereas the caudal-ventral part sends its main efferent projections to the cerebellum and medulla (Samuels and Szabadi, 2008b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to tracer studies.

claim: The caudal-ventral part of the LC sends its main efferent projections to the cerebellum and medulla.
source: Tracer studies show that the rostral-dorsal part of the LC projects to neocortical regions, the hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, and amygdala, whereas the caudal-ventral part sends its main efferent projections to the cerebellum and medulla (Samuels and Szabadi, 2008b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to tracer studies.

claim: The study provides an in vivo account of LC functional projections, revealing that the connections most reproducible across cohorts, mainly from the rostral part, are in reasonable agreement with anatomical connectivity studies.
source: Here, we provide an in vivo account of LC functional projections, revealing that the connections most reproducible across cohorts, mainly from the rostral part, are in reasonable agreement with anatomical connectivity studies, and these connections drive the gradient of functional connectivity throughout the LC.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings in relation to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The connections most reproducible across cohorts drive the gradient of functional connectivity throughout the LC.
source: Here, we provide an in vivo account of LC functional projections, revealing that the connections most reproducible across cohorts, mainly from the rostral part, are in reasonable agreement with anatomical connectivity studies, and these connections drive the gradient of functional connectivity throughout the LC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about what drives the observed gradient.

claim: In addition to tracer studies, the caudal part of the LC also shows connectivity to primary sensorimotor and visual cortical regions, as well as the thalami.
source: However, in addition to tracer studies, we found that the caudal part also shows connectivity to primary sensorimotor and visual cortical regions, as well as the thalami.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that extends beyond previous tracer studies.

claim: Some regions showing caudal LC connectivity, especially the thalami, were reported to show connectivity with the LC in previous fMRI studies.
source: Some of these regions, especially the thalami, were reported to show connectivity with the LC in previous fMRI studies (Liebe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous fMRI research.

claim: It is possible that downstream multisynaptic connections in primary sensorimotor and visual regions reflect the cerebellar projections of the caudal LC, since the cerebellum is known to have strong reciprocal connections to multiple thalamic nuclei and primary sensorimotor cortical areas.
source: Regarding primary sensorimotor and visual regions, it is possible that downstream multisynaptic connections in these regions reflect the cerebellar projections of the caudal LC, since the cerebellum is known to have strong reciprocal connections to multiple thalamic nuclei and primary sensorimotor cortical areas (Caligiore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation about cerebellar connectivity.

claim: The fMRI acquisition in the CamCAN cohort did not cover the entire cerebellum and upper cervical spinal cord.
source: It is important to note that the fMRI acquisition in the CamCAN cohort did not cover the entire cerebellum and upper cervical spinal cord, which are known targets of projections in the caudal LC, therefore we did not investigate them in this study.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The cerebellum and upper cervical spinal cord are known targets of projections in the caudal LC.
source: It is important to note that the fMRI acquisition in the CamCAN cohort did not cover the entire cerebellum and upper cervical spinal cord, which are known targets of projections in the caudal LC, therefore we did not investigate them in this study.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LC anatomy and connectivity.

claim: Electrophysiological studies report non-overlapping spontaneous activation dynamics from different sites in the LC that associate with and drive different cortical states.
source: Electrophysiological studies report non-overlapping spontaneous activation dynamics from different sites in the LC that associate with and drive different cortical states, suggesting the presence of distinct neural ensembles in the LC that regulate multiple cortical states, instead of a homogeneous arousal-related release of noradrenaline across the cortex (Noei et al., 2022).
